Currently, there are three major configurations of sCO power cycles that are actively being 2 researched: (i) simple, (ii) recompression, and (iii) partial cooling, shown in Figure 2 (Neises et al. 2019). Figure 2. sCO2 cycle configurations The simple cycle consists of a turbine (T), a main compressor (MC), a primary heat exchanger (PHX), a low-temperature recuperator (LTR), and a cooler. The recuperator transfers heat from the turbine exhaust to the high-pressure cold compressor outlet. The heat transfer fluid adds heat to the cycle through the PHX. In the recompression configuration, a recompressor (RC) bypasses some flow around the cooler, MC, and LTR before mixing with the mainstream after the LTR. Additionally, this configuration contains a second recuperator that handles the high-temperature recuperation (HTR). This configuration aims to improve on the simple cycle efficiency by more effective recuperation in the LTR. In the partial cooling sCO cycle configuration, a second 2 cooler and first-stage compressor are added after the LTR and before the recompression flow spilt. This configuration typically operates over higher pressure ratios and larger temperatures difference across the turbine than recompression. The introduction of PCMs within the HTF will impact PHX 2 design and performance. Here we discuss our modeling methodology of the PHX, which allows us to capture the impact of proposed PCM particles increasing the heat capacity of the HTF driving the sCO cycle. 2 The PHX model assumes a counterflow configuration and uses a sub-heat exchanger modeling approach. In this approach, the PHX is discretized into smaller heat exchangers, heat transfer is assumed to be constant for each sub-heat exchanger (i.e., total required heat transfer divided by the number of sub-heat exchangers), and NTU-effectiveness relationships (conductance ratio method) are used to estimate the required heat exchanger conductance (Nellis et al. 2008).
